newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Occidental says Colombia army protection failing.
newsitem.headline: Occidental says Colombia army protection failing.

text.p: Leftist rebel attacks on Colombia's key oil infrastructure are intensifying while the army's response to the growing threat is inadequate, Occidental Petroleum Corp officials said Monday.
The U.S. multinational shut in production and declared force majeure early Monday at the Cano Limon field it operates in northeast Arauca province for the second time in three weeks.
The move came in the wake of a spate of rebel bombings and a landslide which partially destroyed the main pipeline that transports crude from the field to the port of Covenas on the Caribbean coast.

"These (attacks) are a clear indication that things are getting worse," an Occidental spokesman told Reuters. "Of course we see room for improvement in the ability of the military to guarantee security in the area."

The Cano Limon-Covenas pipeline has been blown up by national Liberation Army (ELN) rebels 45 times this year with the spillage of more than 140,000 barrels of crude. It was bombed the same number of times in the whole of last year and 105,000 barrels of oil were spilled.
In contrast to more isolated attacks in the past which only succeeded in halting pumping for brief periods, the ELN have adopted the tactic of dynamiting the line several times within a few days.
This has obliged Occidental to declare force majeure on production twice in three weeks -- the only two times since the field opened more than 10 years ago.

The growing success of the ELN in launching its devastating attacks has also exposed flaws in military strategy. Armed forces chief Gen. Manuel Jose Bonett estimates at least 11,000 soldiers, of the army's active combat force of about 100,000 men, are deployed in protecting oil infrastructure.
But the guerrillas have stepped up their attacks and last month killed 30 soldiers in two separate firefights as they moved in to aid pipeline repairs.
The Occidental spokesman said the latest wave of bombings should not be seen as a rebel victory.
"I cannot call this a triumph for the guerrilla because we have to take into account the lost royalties and lost employment," he said.
The declaration of force majeure in the Cano Limon field means the temporary suspension of contracts for contractors and some full time workers, affecting a total of about 200 people.
Despite the problems, Occidental, which averages 175,000 barrels per day output from Cano Limon, is not contemplating pulling out.
"In no way are we considering leaving. We're an experienced operation and we understand the peculiar risks of operating here," the spokesman said.
